items.title: Don't Forget the Keyboard
items.note: Laptop performance, typed music, and where notepat and AC Native OS stand · 68-source platter
items.text: Don't Forget the Keyboard maps twenty years of laptop performance and forty of QWERTY note entry: typewriter percussion, tracker piano rows, Roblox letter sheets, PLOrk and the native-input program, six key-mapping logics, typing as the gesture, the liveness critique, and computers booted into instruments. It tests four claims about Aesthetic.Computer against that map. Two survive narrowly, one is measured, one is argued, and each comes with the study that would settle it.

items.title: iOS So Far
items.text: Ten years of apps on Apple’s store, read through reviews, sales, release history, and the work still needed to ship.

items.title: Eat the Right Answer
items.note: Gaming and education, tested against the nom drills, KidLisp cards, and the oskiewar coach · 6pp
items.text: Eat the Right Answer reads three objects built inside Aesthetic.Computer against the games-and-learning literature: the nom family of muncher drills, whose June paper's prediction is tested against three months of commits; KidLisp cards, a program on a card handed to a UCLA cohort; and the oskiewar coach, a spectator process that never presses a button and keeps a ledger for a model. All three share a seam: a fixed engine, a swappable table, and a watcher on the outside. The drill has no watcher. That is the next table to write.

items.title: Free Versus Nonfree
items.note: Stallman's licensing map and where Aesthetic.Computer stands · 6pp
items.text: Free Versus Nonfree reconstructs Stallman's map of software licensing from his 1998 essay and its 2007 rewrite: one ethical line drawn by four freedoms, copyleft versus lax inside it, commerce as a separate axis. It then applies the map to this repository and finds it source-available, not yet free.

items.title: Aesthetic Network Traffic Report
items.text: A traffic audit across sixteen domains, separating human visits from bots, monitoring, and internal requests.

items.title: Taking Turf
items.text: How Aesthetic Computer can find its footing on an internet increasingly written and read by machines.

items.title: Close of August '26
items.text: Recovering a song whose source disappeared, and rebuilding a release around the recording that survived.

items.title: Take the Psychology Out of Posting: the oskiewar Reel Factory
items.text: A four-stage pipeline turning a date into a recorded game, a dressed video, and a checked Instagram Reel.

items.title: The Door Is Shut: oskiewar and the Retail Xbox Store
items.text: What separates a working Developer Mode Xbox game from retail distribution: packaging, platform integration, and the GDK port.

items.title: oskiewar
items.text: A fighting-game laboratory connecting native Xbox play, browser spectation, spatial sound, and compact replays.

items.title: ProPublica — A Dossier
items.note: 501(c)(3) investigative newsroom · IRS 990 + accountability record · arXiv
items.text: What is publicly recoverable about ProPublica: origin, nonprofit structure, newsroom and partner network, data tools, people, money, reach, awards, corrections, and disputed work. Fact-surfacing, not argument.

items.title: Equal Enough to Draw
items.note: Paths, Equivalence, and Evidence in a Tiny Creative Language · arXiv 7pp
items.text: Equal Enough to Draw studies what homotopy type theory can honestly contribute to KidLisp without pretending the live language is a proof assistant. It separates source, AST, render, trace, contextual, and type-level identity; defines bounded observational equivalence over a host, input trace, frame horizon, and tolerance; and proposes content-addressed path certificates beside the permissive paint loop.

items.title: A Record in the Mail
items.note: An essay on API-made vinyl and cassette fulfillment · podcast
items.text: A podcast asks to become an object. This essay maps two routes from an Aesthetic Computer episode to the mailbox: Kunaki's product-and-order API for one-off vinyl, and Tape On Demand's more human cassette workflow. It argues for a shared physical-release manifest, a deliberate payment gate, and a side B that can turn physical media into correspondence.

items.title: Stack of the Summer '26
items.note: A Nine-Vector Platform Report · arXiv-style · Summer 2026
items.text: Stack of the Summer '26 cuts through Aesthetic Computer's living platform: the piece lifecycle and creative runtime, user data and backend choices, realtime and deployment, KidLisp publishing, shared services, desktop and bare-metal embodiments, engineering quality, privacy boundaries, and architectural history. It distinguishes canonical, transitional, and experimental layers, then names the priorities that can thicken the platform without losing its narrow creative waist.

items.title: The Console Has a Browser
items.text: What a browser on a game console reveals about controller identity, compatibility, and the web as a game platform.

items.title: The Record Is a Better Interface
items.note: An essay on expressive playback · podcast
items.text: A turntable lets a listener hold recorded sound directly, while streaming apps reduce playback to a menu of approved speeds. This essay asks why production tools remain instruments while consumer players became transport controls, and argues for audible, continuous scrubbing that gives the recording back to the hand.

items.title: Gaps in Granularity
items.note: Expressive Control and the Impoverishment of Consumer Playback · arXiv 10pp
items.text: A record scratch gives you continuous, gestural, real-time control over a recording; YouTube and Spotify give you a dropdown of round speeds, and some give nothing at all. This paper names that gap 'granularity,' grounds it in the theory of directness and the mature craft of turntablism and elastic audio, and shows that Aesthetic Computer already ships the alternative across its players. The real opening is not that the instrument is impossible, but that it lives everywhere except the default transport of the apps you actually listen and watch through.

items.title: Aesthinema
items.text: Making generative cinema with consistent characters, canonical reference images, and human approvals.

items.title: 'Sup w/ July 10?
items.note: Essay · ~2pp · mid-month postcard · podcast
items.text: A mid-month postcard from July 10th --- not the monthly essay but a check-in written because someone asked how it was going. The answer: living in two times at once. Told as three scenes: excavating Whistlegraph, an artform made years ago with a friend, now counted (963 videos transcribed, 424 songs clustered, ~1.72 billion views) and given a hand-lettered legal-pad home at whistlegraph.org; a brand-new fighting game, fight, born in two days with its rollback safety net built before its network floor; and Menuband bounced from App Store review for naming macOS in its subtitle, then let through after learning to say one word less. Also available as a spoken reading in @jeffrey's voice.

items.title: The Media Estate
items.note: One Funnel, Nine Surfaces · 16:9 deck 10pp
items.text: An overview deck of the Aesthetic Computer and whistlegraph media estate: twelve accounts across nine surfaces, which can be posted to by script today, and the build-out plan. The whistlegraph archive still moves tens of thousands of views a day; the deck argues the work is connecting that audience to the new instrument, starting with Instagram.

items.title: Aesthetic July 4 '26
items.note: Essay · ~4pp · Independence Day special
items.text: An Independence Day special between the June and July essays, written on the Declaration's 250th anniversary. Independence is a hanging word --- in + dependere, not to hang from --- and the essay follows it in the abstract: declarations versus definitions in C and in Philadelphia, the personal computer as an independence movement the cloud quietly reversed, artists who built their own rooms (a library in a church, folk songs as open-source software, an artwork designed to scan badly), and an honest ledger of which way one small platform hangs --- a podcast hung from a host, Menuband submitted to App Store review on the holiday weekend itself, and the CNAME record as infrastructure's most truthful sentence.

items.title: Aesthetic June '26
items.note: Essay · ~3pp · podcast
items.text: Aesthetic June '26 is the storytelling companion to May. Where May was the modal mood, June is the answer, delivered as four hundred and fifty-seven commits --- the word carrying both its meanings, version control and Juno's oath. Told as scenes: the songs that caught up, the whistle found a perfect fifth sharp, the ring of native wizards learning one sign-in, and a Danish learn-the-clock community getting its own front door on the chat. Also available as a spoken reading in @jeffrey's voice.

items.title: The Pals Mark
items.text: The history and evolution of the Aesthetic Computer logo.

items.title: The Keymap Is the Score
items.note: A plain-spoken companion to Keymaps as Social Software · essay
items.text: A keymap is more than a hidden preference table: it is an agreement that travels between people, programs, and machines. This essay names the inherited AWSED piano layout, introduces notepat's notes-that-name-themselves alternative, and follows that argument into the hand-assembled Scores for Social Software edition at UCLA.

items.title: AesthetiCal: A URL-Addressable Calendar
items.note: A URL-Addressable Calendar for Aesthetic Computer · arXiv 6pp
items.text: AesthetiCal adds time to Aesthetic Computer as a piece, not a second app: month/week/day views and a DateWizard share a per-handle synced store, addressable by permahandle and interchangeable as standard iCalendar. The paper describes the shipped v1 and sketches the next phase — bookable shows, invites, and the Aestheticks ticketing tie-in.

items.title: The Hand and the Loop
items.note: Three Eras of My Own Code: Hand-Written, GPT-Grafted, Agentic · arXiv 4pp
items.text: The Hand and the Loop reads AC's git history across three eras — hand-written, GPT-grafted, and fully agentic — and asks honestly whether the codebase is better off. It weighs 5x velocity and five new subsystems against the loss of instrument-like minimalism, and argues for keeping the loop in the leaves while a human hand carves the foundational libraries.

items.title: The nom Games
items.note: Muncher Arcade for Aesthetic Computer · arXiv
items.text: The nom games rebuild MECC's Word and Number Munchers as Aesthetic Computer pieces --- numbnom, engnom, mexinom, and notenom. The paper shows how one shared engine and a reusable virtual synth controller turn each new subject or language into a content table rather than a new game, with the answer key in notenom doubling as a playable instrument.

items.title: Aesthetic May '26
items.note: Essay · ~5pp
items.text: Aesthetic May '26 is a magazine-style essay companion to Five Years from Now. May is both the month and the modal verb of possibility; the essay reads the present as a field of branching maybes rather than a line of probabilities --- where the music lane may go, what jeffrey may do, what may not happen this year, and the weather acting on all of it. First entry in the essay-* lane.

items.title: Keymaps as Social Software
items.text: Keyboard layouts as shared, versioned musical agreements that travel between people and applications.

items.title: Diagrams from Data
items.text: Generating reproducible diagrams from repository data with Penrose and a deterministic TikZ fallback.

items.title: Where the Microseconds Go
items.text: Tracing the keypress-to-sound path through AC Native OS, from USB interrupts to audio hardware.Venue edition: papers/siggraph-asia-2026-tech. No submission receipt in mail (checked 2026-10-15).

items.title: The URL Tradition
items.note: Addressable Creative Computing from Lovelace's Footnotes to Aesthetic Computer · arXiv
items.text: The URL Tradition traces address-thinking from Lovelace's footnotes, Bush's trails, Xanadu, and the Negro Motorist Green Book through net.art, single-serving sites, the tilde, Glitch, and Aesthetic Computer's prompt-as-address-bar. It argues the URL is not a feature but a medium property that reshapes authorship, distribution, pedagogy, performance, and political claim.

items.title: The Potter and the Prompt
items.note: John Holden's Proto-Cognitive Music Theory and Aesthetic Computer · arXiv 7pp
items.text: The Potter and the Prompt argues that AC independently converges on the core principles of John Holden's 1770 proto-cognitive music theory. It proposes AC as a computational laboratory for advancing Holden's unfinished program on grouping, attention, and the module.

items.title: Who Pays for Creative Tools?
items.note: Funding, Burnout, and Survival in Open-Source Creative Computing · arXiv 5pp
items.text: A short look at who supports open-source creative tools and what that labor costs. The paper connects funding, burnout, and long-term maintenance to the life of artistic software.

items.title: Two Departments, One Building
items.text: Two Departments, One Building examines how funding and infrastructure shape creative work in shared spaces. The paper looks at administrative boundaries as part of the artistic system.

items.title: Handle Identity on the AT Protocol
items.text: Handle Identity on the AT Protocol treats naming as a social and technical problem. The paper explores how handles, identity, and publishing can be tied together without losing portability.

items.title: KidLisp Language Reference
items.note: 118 Built-ins in 12 Categories · arXiv 4pp
items.text: The KidLisp reference compresses the language into a usable field guide. It groups 118 built-ins into 12 categories for quick browsing and recall.

items.title: CalArts, Callouts, and Papers
items.text: CalArts, Callouts, and Papers turns a local institutional context into a study of friction, attention, and production. The paper leans into psycho style to show how academic labor is staged and performed.

items.title: Five Years from Now
items.text: Five Years from Now is a projection paper about where the project could go if current habits continue. It uses the near future to test the consequences of today's decisions.

items.title: Get Closed Source Out of Schools
items.text: Get Closed Source Out of Schools makes the case that creative computing should be teachable, inspectable, and modifiable. The paper argues for open tools as infrastructure for learning.

items.title: KidLisp Cards
items.text: KidLisp Cards condenses the language into a pocketable card format. It is meant to make the language easier to browse, teach, and carry.

items.title: Reading the Score
items.text: Reading the Score looks at the graphic score as an interface for interpretation and collaboration. The paper treats notation as a computational and social object.

items.title: PLOrk'ing the Planet
items.note: Laptop Orchestras, PLOrk Heritage, and Aesthetic Computer · arXiv
items.text: This paper connects Aesthetic Computer to laptop orchestras and the collaborative traditions of PLOrk. It treats the browser as a place for ensemble practice, not just solo desktop programming.

items.title: Sucking on the Complex
items.note: Platform Hegemony, Critique-as-Content, and Anti-Environments · arXiv 5pp
items.text: Sucking on the Complex critiques platform hegemony and the way critique becomes content. It looks for anti-environments that stay messy, resistant, and alive.

items.title: Playable Folk Songs
items.note: Oral Tradition Meets the Browser Keyboard · arXiv
items.text: Playable Folk Songs brings oral tradition into the browser keyboard. The paper asks how simple interaction can carry collective memory and repetition.

items.title: From setup() to boot()
items.note: Processing at the Core of the Piece API · arXiv 7pp
items.text: The Piece API rethinks creative software around composable pieces instead of monolithic apps. It uses Processing's lineage to connect setup(), boot(), and the act of publishing.

items.title: KidLisp (ELS 2026)
items.note: A Minimal Lisp for Generative Art with Social Composition · ELS ACM SIGS 4pp
items.text: An ELS conference version of KidLisp that emphasizes social composition. It positions the language as a shared practice rather than a solo scripting environment.No submission receipt in mail (checked 2026-10-15).

items.title: Network Audit
items.note: Who Uses Aesthetic Computer and What Do They Make? · arXiv 4pp
items.text: Network Audit asks who uses Aesthetic Computer and what they make with it. The paper turns usage patterns into a portrait of a community in motion.

items.title: Citation Diversity Audit
items.note: Diversity and Inclusion in AC Paper Citations · 4pp
items.text: Citation Diversity Audit looks at who gets cited in the papers and where the archive is thin. The paper uses citation patterns as a proxy for inclusion and intellectual range.

items.title: Radical Computer Art
items.note: Goodiepalian Approaches in Aesthetic Computer · arXiv 5pp
items.text: This paper treats Goodiepalian practice as a model for radical computer art. It emphasizes play, notation, and the social life of systems over polished product design.

items.title: Vestigial Features
items.note: Dormant Paths, Evolutionary Branches, and Abandoned Approaches · arXiv 4pp
items.text: The paper catalogs dormant branches, abandoned experiments, and paths that never became default. It treats dead ends as useful history rather than failure.

items.title: Whistlegraph
items.note: Drawing, Singing, and the Graphic Score as Viral Form · arXiv 4pp
items.text: Whistlegraph explores drawing, singing, and score-making as forms that can spread like software. The paper links graphic notation to performance, remix, and browser-native sharing.

items.title: AC Native OS
items.note: A Bare-Metal Creative Computing Operating System · arXiv 5pp
items.text: AC Native OS describes a bare-metal runtime for creative computing. It focuses on boot-time simplicity and the idea that the operating system itself can be a programmable art surface.

items.title: Repository Archaeology
items.note: Tracing the Evolution of AC Through Its Git History · arXiv 3pp · interactive timeline
items.text: Repository Archaeology traces the project through its git history. The paper shows how version control can become a narrative medium for design evolution.

items.title: notepat.com
items.note: From Keyboard Toy to System Front Door · arXiv 5pp
items.text: notepat.com is framed as a keyboard-first front door to the system. The paper follows the toy-like input surface as it grows into a fuller creative interface.

items.title: Pieces Not Programs
items.note: The Piece as a Unit of Creative Cognition · arXiv 4pp
items.text: A piece is treated here as the basic unit of creative cognition in AC. The paper argues that smaller, shareable pieces encourage composition, remix, and publication.

items.title: Aesthetic Computer '26
items.note: A Mobile-First Runtime for Creative Computing · arXiv 5pp
items.text: Aesthetic Computer is presented as a mobile-first creative computing runtime where the interface, publishing flow, and community feedback loop are part of the medium. The paper argues that small pieces can make software feel more social, more portable, and easier to share.Venue edition: papers/cc-demo-2026. No submission receipt in mail (checked 2026-10-15).

items.title: Aesthetic Computer '26
items.note: JOSS Summary · 2pp
items.text: A compact JOSS summary of Aesthetic Computer for archival and citation purposes. It distills the platform into a conventional software paper format.

items.title: KidLisp '26
items.note: A Minimal Lisp for Generative Art on a Social Platform · arXiv 6pp
items.text: KidLisp is the platform's tiny Lisp for building visual and musical pieces in the browser. The paper shows how a minimal language can stay approachable while still supporting generative art and composition.Venue edition: papers/iccc-kidlisp. No submission receipt in mail (checked 2026-10-15).

items.title: KidLisp '26
items.note: JOSS Summary · 3pp
items.text: A compact JOSS summary of KidLisp for archival and citation purposes. It frames the language as a small but expressive tool for generative art.
